and that there should be peace.
And al-Ashraf did not accept,
but set out from Mosul and crossed the Tigris,
and went and encamped in Salamiyyah, a village near the river Zab.
And Muzaffar al-Din was encamped on the other side of the Zab.
Now Nasir al-Din, the lord of Amid,
because he too was with al-Ashraf,
and had a secret affection for Muzaffar al-Din,
counseled al-Malik al-Ashraf to make peace and return with honor.
And he said to him further:
"If you conquer,
you will offend the Caliph and be blamed by the whole community;
and if you are defeated,
it will be an evil name for you and for those who are with you forever."
And al-Ashraf was persuaded and consented to peace;
and he took 'Imad al-Din Zangi, the lord of 'Aqr, with him as a hostage until he should surrender the fortresses which he had taken,
and he returned and went to Sinjar.
And certain men went to take the fortresses from him
and surrender them to the house of Badr al-Din.
And except for one fortress within the border of the Hakkari Kurds, they were not able to take any,
because the rest of them
showed rebellion and refused to surrender.
Muzaffar al-Din Zangi cast himself upon Shihab al-Din Ghazi, the brother of al-Ashraf,
and he interceded with al-Ashraf on his behalf,
and he let him be without surrendering the fortresses.
And Badr al-Din was grieved at this,
but he was not able to stand against the will of al-Ashraf.
And at that time, Badr al-Din perceived
that al-Ashraf was waiting to take Tell 'Afar from him,
because it had formerly belonged to Sinjar.
Therefore, he sent and surrendered Tell 'Afar to him,
and Sinjar together with Tell 'Afar belonged to al-Ashraf.
Now when Zangi took control over all the fortresses of the Hakkaris and of the Zawzanites, he began to ill-treat the people in them,
and oppressed
them with exactions.
And on this account, those who had kept the covenant with him repented,
and they wished to surrender to Badr al-Din,
but they were afraid because of the opposition which they had shown.
